title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Detroit limits new data centers to protect grids and neighborhoods—what it means for bills statewide.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Tuesday, August 11, and our big story today is Detroit's new policy capping data centers at small scale to avoid straining local grids.
That sounds like a big shift from what we've seen in other states. Graham, what's the core of this new city rule?

Detroit is keeping new facilities from growing into massive power users. The policy sets limits so they don't pull hundreds of megawatts that could drive up rates or create noise issues for neighbors.
Why does this matter right now? We've heard about fights in places like Saline and Marshall.
Exactly. Residents in Detroit avoid the heavy electricity rate hikes and noise problems reported elsewhere. It protects neighborhood character while still allowing some limited tech growth.
How did we get here? Was there a specific history or previous proposals that pushed the city to act?
This builds on broader concerns we've tracked. Cities across Michigan are watching what happens when big projects land without guardrails.
Who are the main players here? City officials, residents, or the tech companies pushing for bigger sites?
It's the city setting the rules, responding to resident worries about grid strain and local impacts. Developers still get a path forward, just not the giant campuses seen in other states.
What about electric bills? Could this keep rates steadier for Detroiters compared to areas with larger projects?
That's the hope. By capping scale, the city aims to prevent the kind of demand spikes that force utilities to upgrade infrastructure and pass costs to everyone.
Water use is another big issue with these facilities. Does the Detroit rule touch on that at all?
The focus is mainly on power and scale right now, but smaller facilities generally mean less overall resource demand, including water for cooling.
Farmland and rural towns often get pulled into these debates too. How does a city policy like this ripple out?
Detroit's move could set a precedent. Other communities are already looking at similar limits to keep projects from overwhelming small-town infrastructure.
What happens next? Will more cities follow Detroit's lead, or is this an outlier?
We'll watch the upcoming meetings in places like Lowell and Portage. The trend toward tighter rules seems to be gaining steam statewide.
Any sense of how developers are reacting to these caps?
They'll likely adjust proposals to fit the smaller scale, or look to communities with looser rules for now.
And for ratepayers 30 miles away, why should they care about what Detroit does?
Regional grids are connected. Keeping one major city from adding huge loads helps stabilize costs across the area.
Got it. This feels like a proactive step rather than reacting after a big project is already approved.
That's the key difference here.
Let's move to some quick hits on other developments today. Graham, what's the latest out of Mount Pleasant?
The Mount Pleasant data center contract still includes a power plant provision that Wisconsin regulators already struck down. That raises the risk of higher local energy costs if it moves forward.
Interesting how an out-of-state fight ends up shaping Michigan bills. Lowell is also in the news.
Officials there say new zoning and permitting standards won't be ready for several more months, leaving proposals to move under current weaker rules.
Residents won't have much say on power and water demands until then. Switching to Whitehall Township.
Supervisors there reviewed a new ordinance setting limits on size, noise, and power use in a rural area. It could affect taxes and grid strain depending on what passes.
Kalamazoo is weighing a year-long freeze. What's the plan there?
City leaders will debate a moratorium at their next meeting to block proposals while they study power and water demands.
That pause would give time to write rules before anything breaks ground. Up in the U.P., locals are teaming with a comedian.
Residents are pushing back against proposed AI data centers that could strain grids and water. Comedian Charlie Berens is amplifying their concerns.
Marshall approved its own one-year moratorium. How does that help?
It halts all proposals for at least 12 months so planners can study impacts on power and noise. Residents get breathing room.
Yesterday brought a court battle in Oakland County. Graham, fill us in.
A developer sued after a suburb imposed a temporary halt on new projects. The case will test how far local governments can go in pausing large facilities.
And Attorney General Nessel is appealing a DTE deal for a Saline data center.
She and environmental groups filed arguments challenging the contract over whether costs are fairly allocated. Higher bills could hit locals if it stands.
Michigan Advance also had a roundup on tax and power fights this week.
It tracks active battles over incentives, grid upgrades, and water use that affect ratepayers statewide.
Now for on deck. Graham, what meetings can listeners actually attend today?
Lowell Township Planning Commission is discussing a proposal for a data center ordinance this evening.
And Portage City Council has a data center industrial zoning discussion on the agenda.
Both are chances for residents to weigh in directly.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Detroit Caps Data Centers at Small Scale; Moratoriums Spread Across Michigan
